pages.title: About
pages.content:
Founded in 2017 by registered nurse Mira Castell, Tayori Nursing began with the conviction that clinical care belongs in familiar surroundings where everyday life unfolds. Operating from an office at 14 Orchard Row in Linden Vale, the service was created to support individuals within an 8 km radius who require steady medical attention at home. The name Tayori reflects this purpose, signifying someone dependable to turn to during times of illness, recovery, or physical change.

Over the years, the practice expanded to assemble a dedicated multidisciplinary team comprising registered nurses, a physiotherapist, an occupational therapist, and a care-plan coordinator. Rather than offering hurried or impersonal appointments, the team structured visits around unhurried kitchen-table assessments and regular daytime rounds. By introducing a 24-hour on-call support line for registered patients, Tayori Nursing established a continuous, dependable bridge between hospital discharge and daily home living.

Today, Tayori Nursing continues to serve Linden Vale households seven days a week between 8:00 and 20:00. Whether helping an older adult regain independent mobility after surgery, administering ongoing wound therapies, or providing gentle palliative care, the team remains committed to the same founding standard established in 2017: delivering calm, professional nursing right to your living room.

pages.title: Contact
pages.content:
Tayori Nursing, 14 Orchard Row, Linden Vale. Phone +1 555 0147, mail hello@tayori-nursing.example.

Office hours: Mon–Sat 8:30–18:00 (closed Sundays and public holidays). Visit hours: 7 days, 8:00–20:00. The 24-hour on-call line is for registered patients only.

We visit homes within 8 km of the office, about 20 minutes by bicycle or car. In an emergency call your local emergency number.

posts.title: A morning round on Orchard Row
posts.excerpt: What the first four hours of a visiting day look like, stop by stop.
posts.content:
The briefing at 8:00 is short: who is on the list, who needs a longer visit, and who we promised to call back. By 8:40 the first nurse is at a front door with a blood-pressure cuff and the morning medicines list.

Between visits there is rarely a car park. Most of the round is walked or cycled, which is how we notice the things a clinic never sees: a loose rug, a full bin, a neighbour who calls in with soup.

posts.title: Why we write the plan at the kitchen table
posts.excerpt: The care plan is agreed at home, on paper, with the family if you wish.
posts.content:
A plan written in an office is a plan about a patient. A plan written at the kitchen table is a plan with a person, who points out that Thursday is the day the grandchildren come and mornings are better than afternoons.

We write it within three days of the assessment visit, you sign it, and it goes to your doctor. Every 30 days we sit down again and change whatever has stopped fitting.

posts.title: A new evening visit slot
posts.excerpt: Visits now run until 20:00, seven days a week.
posts.content:
From this autumn our visiting hours run from 8:00 to 20:00 every day. Early or late visits, before 8:30 or after 18:00, carry a $15 supplement per visit; the written estimate you receive at the assessment visit shows it plainly.

The 24-hour on-call line stays as it was, for registered patients only, at $30 a month.

posts.title: Walking to the bakery again
posts.excerpt: Six weeks of rehabilitation visits, written as the experience of one patient.
posts.content:
Rosa came home after a hip operation unsure about the stairs. Her physiotherapist visited, practised standing and walking with her, and each week the route grew by a few doors.

This is one patient’s experience, not a promise: every plan is different, and every plan is agreed with you first.
